{{Short description|Mathematical rule}}
The '''shift rule''' is a mathematical rule for [[sequence]]s and [[series (mathematics)|series]].

Here <math>n</math> and <math>N</math> are [[natural numbers]]. 

For sequences, the rule states that if <math>(a_{n})</math> is a sequence, then it [[Convergent series|converge]]s [[if and only if]] <math>(a_{n+N})</math> also converges, and in this case both sequences always converge to the same number.<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.ueltschi.org/teaching/2011-MA131/notes-MA131.pdf|title=Analysis –MA131|first=Daniel|last=Ueltschi|publisher=University of Warwick|year=2011|page=31}}.</ref>

For series, the rule states that the series <math>\sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n}</math> converges to a number if and only if <math>\sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n+N}</math> converges.<ref>{{citation|title=How to Think About Analysis|first=Lara|last=Alcock|authorlink= Lara Alcock |publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2014|isbn=9780191035371|page=102|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gk5uBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA102}}.</ref>
